Below is a verse-by-verse commentary on Proverbs 6, drawn from the sources I was able to access within the search and fetch limits. Each point is followed by its source URL. Due to search/fetch limits, I was unable to retrieve Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarly, or tradition-specific (Lutheran, Methodist, etc.) material for this chapter. Those sections are therefore absent.

---

## Proverbs 6 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1
**"My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, if you have struck hands in pledge with a stranger…"**

- The warning is against **rash suretyship** — becoming a guarantor for another person’s debt. This was not an absolute prohibition (Paul did something similar for Onesimus, Philemon 1:18–19), but counsel against doing it without careful thought and with someone not well-known. The "stranger" (Hebrew *zar*) probably refers to a neighbor who is not well-known, a high-risk person. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary)
- Ellicott explains that at the time of Solomon, with Israel’s commerce greatly expanded, lending on interest and suretyship had become common. The Mosaic Law originally forbade lending at interest to the poor (Leviticus 25:35–37), but commercial loans were a different matter. The danger was that the surety made himself liable for debts he could not control. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- Gill notes that "striking hands" was a gesture used in suretyship for confirmation, like a handshake sealing a deal. The caution is against entering such an arrangement rashly, without knowing the person or considering whether one can afford to pay without hurting one's family. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/6.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that the phrase "for a stranger" uses the Hebrew *zar*, meaning "one extraneous to oneself" — someone with whom one is but slightly acquainted, not a foreign national. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/6.htm)

### v. 2
**"if you have been trapped by the words of your lips, ensnared by the words of your mouth…"**

- The key word is "words of your mouth." Your own promise has become a snare. Kidner notes this was more like guaranteeing someone’s open line of credit than cosigning a modern loan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary)
- Matthew Henry says the caution teaches that a man should never be surety for more than he is able and willing to pay without wronging his family; he ought to look upon every sum he is engaged for as his own debt. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-6.html)
- Bridges makes a gospel connection: "Our God, while he warns us against putting up security, has taken it on himself… He has given us his Word, his bond, yes, his blood as security for sinners." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary)

### v. 3
**"then do this, my son, to free yourself… Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor."**

- The advice is urgent: if you are trapped, **humble yourself** before the creditor or the friend for whom you pledged. Poole notes the Hebrew implies "offer thyself to be trodden upon, or throw thyself down at his feet." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary)
- The NET Bible note explains the verb rendered "humble yourself" (Hebrew *raphas*) means "to stamp oneself down" — swallowing pride, being unremitting in effort. The verb rendered "press your plea" (*rahav*) means "to act stormily, to importune," i.e., be bold and don't take no for an answer. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary)
- Ellicott: "Thou hast made thy freedom and property dependent on him for whom thou hast become surety." The solution is to humbly sue for release and to assail impetuously (importune) the friend to pay his debt. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- The Believer's Study Bible (cited by Precept Austin) notes that the creditor now holds surety which may include a man's house and goods, making all he has dependent on the will of his creditor-neighbor. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary)

### v. 4
**"Allow no sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids."**

- This is a call to immediate, urgent action — don't procrastinate. The same language is used by David in Psalm 132:4–5 about finding a place for the Lord. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-6-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/6.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary says the appeal is not to be one spasmodic effort and then abandoned; the friend is to be followed up "pertinaciously and continually, with unwearied diligence." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/6.htm)

### v. 5
**"Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the snare of the fowler."**

- A gazelle or bird would do anything to escape. The point is the desperation and urgency with which one should seek release from a rash surety obligation. Waltke notes the surety has "handed himself over to the debtor, who may unmercifully throw him into the hands of the creditor." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Garrett adds: "Seizure of assets and home and even the selling of the debtor into slavery were common penalties for failure to make payment, and the cosigner could well have met the same fate." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes a wordplay in the Hebrew between *ts'vi* (roe/gazelle) and *tsippor* (bird). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/6.htm)

### vv. 6–8
**"Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise. Without a commander, without an overseer or ruler, it prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest."**

- The ant is proverbial for industry. Adam Clarke: "No insect is more laborious, not even the bee itself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- The key lesson: the ant works **without needing external pressure** — no captain, overseer, or ruler. True diligence comes from within. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- The Pulpit Commentary says the three terms (guide/overseer/ruler) correspond to judge, scribe/official, and prince/ruler — yet the ant needs none of them. It works independently by common instinct. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/6.htm)
- Trapp (cited by Enduring Word) says: "Christ sends us to school to the birds of the air, and lilies of the field… and to the stork, crane, and swallow, to be taught to take the seasons of grace." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Modern naturalists have confirmed ants organize socially, but as Waltke notes, this does "not imply that there is a hierarchy of command." The ant still illustrates self-motivated diligence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- The Pulpit Commentary devotes extensive space to defending the accuracy of the ant's provident habits, citing ancient writers (Hesiod, Virgil, Horace, Aesop) and modern observations (Darwin on the Texas agricultural ant; Canon Tristram on Palestinian ants active in winter). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/6.htm)

### vv. 9–11
**"How long will you lie there, O slacker? When will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit."**

- Solomon mimics the lazy man: "A little sleep, a little slumber…" The sluggard thinks he only needs a little more rest, but actually he needs to work. Waltke: "Sleep is the defining characteristic of the sluggard… his narcotic sleep ever craves still more sleep to escape the pain of living." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Poverty comes "like a robber" (or "like a prowler / armed man") — suddenly and irresistibly. Adam Clarke: "with irresistible fury; and thou art not prepared to oppose it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- At least 14 proverbs relate idleness to poverty (Waltke). It is not riches the lazy person lacks; it is food, the necessity of life. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Ellicott notes the Hebrew form for "one that travelleth" is intensive — "one who moves swiftly." While the sluggard sleeps, poverty is coming on apace. These verses are repeated in Proverbs 24:33–34. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- Matthew Henry applies it to the soul: "How many love their sleep of sin, and their dreams of worldly happiness! Shall we not seek to awaken such?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/proverbs-6.html)

### vv. 12–15
**"A worthless person, a wicked man, walks with a perverse mouth, winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers. With deceit in his heart he devises evil; he continually sows discord. Therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly…"**

- The "worthless person" is literally "a man of Belial" (Ellicott) — a term for worthlessness and wickedness. His whole body is enlisted in deceit: mouth, eyes, feet, fingers. Ellicott calls it "a picture, taken from the life, of a malicious tattler and scandalmonger, who fills out his lying tale with winks and signs, whereby even more is suggested than he says, to the blasting of his neighbour’s character." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- The ultimate sin is **sowing discord** — this is the climactic seventh sin in the list that follows (v. 19). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Calamity comes "suddenly" and "in an instant he will be shattered beyond recovery" — Ellicott: "Shattered as a potter’s vessel (Isaiah 30:14), without hope of recovery." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- Solomon does not directly attribute the calamity to God's judgment, but it is implied. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)

### vv. 16–19
**"There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to Him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that run swiftly to evil, a false witness who gives false testimony, and one who stirs up discord among brothers."**

- The "six… yes, seven" is a Hebrew numerical literary device (called *middah*) used for emphasis and climax. The seventh item is the culminating worst. It appears also in Proverbs 30 and Amos 1–2. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- G. Campbell Morgan: "The six are first stated, and the seventh is that which results, namely, 'he that soweth discord among brethren.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Most sins are connected to **body parts**: eyes (proud look), tongue (lying), hands (shedding blood), heart (devising evil), feet (running to evil). This echoes Paul's teaching in Romans 6:13 about presenting the members of our body to God for righteousness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- "Haughty eyes": Ellicott says pride is hateful to God "because rendering men unfit to receive grace. Till they acknowledge their weakness, they will not seek for His strength." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- "Hands that shed innocent blood": The phrase "innocent blood" implies there are circumstances where taking life is justified (legitimate death penalty, self-defense). The Bible also teaches that unpunished murder defiles a land (Numbers 35:31–34). David Guzik adds: "This surely includes those who are murdered in the womb." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- "One who sows discord among brethren": Morgan says, "We may take it as an unqualified certainty that no man in whose heart the fear of Jehovah prevails and rules, can ever sow discord among brethren." Adam Clarke describes it as "he who troubles the peace of a family, of a village, of the state." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Matthew Henry: "Those sins are in a special manner provoking to God, which are hurtful to the comfort of human life. These things which God hates, we must hate in ourselves." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/proverbs-6.html)

### v. 20
**"My son, keep your father’s commandment, and do not forsake your mother’s teaching."**

- Solomon returns to a theme from Proverbs 1:8. The father's command and mother's teaching represent both parental wisdom and, by extension, God's Word cherished by godly parents. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Precept Austin notes that in Proverbs 5–7, **each warning against sexual misconduct is prefaced by an admonition to pay attention to God's Word** (5:1–2; 6:20–24; 7:1–5). This is the best defense against immorality. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)
- Ross notes: "Implicit in these verses is the basic understanding that a good home life — i.e., father and mother sharing the rearing of the children together — will go a long way to prevent the youth from falling into immorality." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)

### v. 21
**"Bind them always upon your heart; tie them around your neck."**

- The language echoes Deuteronomy 6:8 and Proverbs 3:3. The binding is **figurative** — treasuring God's word in the heart, not wearing literal phylacteries (as the Pharisees later did, Matthew 23:5). Precept Austin notes the Pharisees took this literally, but Solomon means "fastening" God's Word to the heart through reading, memorizing, meditating, and obeying. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)
- Waltke: "it pictures him memorizing them in such a way that they are permanently impressed on his essential mental and spiritual being that prompts his every action." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Wiersbe suggests "tie them around your neck" also speaks to controlling where the neck turns — a man might be tempted to turn his head and look at a beautiful woman for the purpose of lusting (Matthew 5:27–30). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)

### v. 22
**"When you walk, they will guide you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; when you awake, they will speak to you."**

- God's Word is personified here as a living companion: a **guide** when walking, a **guardian** when sleeping, and a **companion** who speaks when awake. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word): "This Bible is a wonderful talking book; there is a great mass of blessed talk in this precious volume. It has told me a great many of my faults; it would tell you yours if you would let it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- F.B. Meyer (cited by Precept Austin): "The man who meditates on the Word of God by day will not be troubled by evil dreams at night." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)

### v. 23
**"For this commandment is a lamp, this teaching is a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way to life…"**

- This echoes Psalm 119:105 ("Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path"). God's word brings light in darkness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Ellicott develops the thought: the servant of God may feel perplexity as to his duty, with darkness on his path. "But there is always some 'commandment,' or positive order, about which he can have no doubt, calling for his immediate obedience." By following what he does know, he prepares himself for more light. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- "Reproofs of discipline" — the painful corrections of God's Word are actually "the way of life." Bridges: "Its reproofs of instruction — as the discipline of our wayward will — are to us as the way of life." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)

### v. 24
**"to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress."**

- This is the specific purpose of treasuring God's Word in this context: protection from sexual temptation. The "smooth tongue" or "flattering tongue" is the seductress's chief weapon. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Bridges: "Specially valuable is this lamp and light in sensual temptation. Those who choose their own light and wisdom, are sure to fall into a flattering snare." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)

### v. 25
**"Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes."**

- The battle begins in the **heart** — lust starts with thoughts. Waltke notes: "coveting begins by allowing eye contact. Desiring comes into his heart through optical stimulation aroused by 'her beauty,' and more specifically by 'the pupils of her eyes.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Ross: "Eyes are singled out here because the painted eyes and the luring glances are symptoms of seduction (see 2 Kings 9:30)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Precept Austin warns practically: "beware of eye contact whether it is flirtatious or inquisitive." The Puritan William Gurnall advised: "Set a strong guard about thy outward senses. These are Satan's landing-place, especially the eye and ear." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)

### v. 26
**"For the levy of the prostitute is poverty, and the adulteress preys upon your very life."**

- The harlot reduces a man to "a crust of bread" — the lowest level of poverty. The adulteress hunts his "precious life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Some commentators (Garrett) translate this as a comparison: "Although the price of a prostitute may be as much as a loaf of bread, [another] man's wife hunts the precious life." The point is not to endorse prostitution but to show the far greater folly and danger of adultery. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Bridges: "By vain beauty and wanton eyes, many a deluded victim has been brought to a piece of bread." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_620-35_commentary)

### vv. 27–29
**"Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned? Can a man walk on hot coals without scorching his feet? So is he who sleeps with another man’s wife; no one who touches her will go unpunished."**

- The fire metaphors are simple and devastating: adultery is like **embracing fire** or **walking on hot coals** — you will certainly be burned. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Bridges: "It is no good for such a man to later on complain about the strength of the temptation. Why did he not avoid it?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Ellicott: "Shall not be innocent" means "unpunished." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- Poole clarifies the phrase "goes in to his neighbor's wife" means "lieth with her" (as in Genesis 19:31; 29:21, 23), and "touches her" means "hath carnal knowledge of her" (as in Genesis 20:6, 1 Corinthians 7:1). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)

### vv. 30–31
**"Men do not despise the thief if he steals to satisfy his hunger. Yet if caught, he must pay sevenfold; he must give up all the wealth of his house."**

- Solomon contrasts theft driven by hunger with adultery driven by lust. People can understand (if not excuse) a starving thief, but even he must make restitution — "sevenfold" meaning full restitution, possibly exceeding the Law's requirement of two-, four-, or fivefold (Exodus 22). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- Trapp: "The thief steals out of want; the adulterer of wantonness." The adulterer has no such excuse. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- Ellicott: "A man who is driven to theft by poverty is more worthy of pity than disdain; not so the adulterer. Again, the thief can make retribution, while the adulterer can have none to offer." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)

### vv. 32–33
**"He who commits adultery lacks judgment; whoever does so destroys himself. Wounds and dishonor will befall him, and his reproach will never be wiped away."**

- The adulterer "lacks judgment" (literally "lacks heart") — he acts against his own best interest. He "destroys his own soul." The damage is self-inflicted. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- The "reproach" (disgrace) is permanent — "will never be wiped away." This is social and moral disgrace that no amount of restitution can remove, unlike the thief who can pay back what he stole. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)

### vv. 34–35
**"For jealousy enrages a husband, and he will show no mercy in the day of vengeance. He will not be appeased by any ransom, or persuaded by lavish gifts."**

- The jealous rage of the wronged husband is implacable. Ellicott: "jealousy is furious, and cannot be appeased by bribes." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/6.htm)
- No ransom (*kopher*) or lavish gifts can compensate for the violation. The adulterer faces a fury that money cannot quiet. This is presented as a pragmatic warning alongside the moral one. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-6/)
- The Pulpit Commentary's treatment of these verses was not accessible within fetch limits, but the theme is consistent across commentators: adultery carries unique, irreversible consequences that no other sin (even theft) does in the same way.
